title: Reliance Jio Gets Regulatory Green Light for 1,600-Satellite Network, India's First Domestic Challenge to Starlink
excerpt: India's space regulator IN-SPACe has cleared Jio's LEO satellite plan as 'technically sound,' paving the way for a $10–15 billion constellation that could rival SpaceX and Amazon.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Reliance Jio's 1,600-satellite plan is cleared by India's IN-SPACe as technically sound.
  • The constellation aims for 4.5–5 Tbps capacity, surpassing Starlink and Amazon's offerings.
  • Estimated project cost is $10–15 billion, marking a significant investment in India's tech landscape.
  • The proposal includes potential military applications, enhancing national security considerations.

  • India's space regulator IN-SPACe has found Reliance Jio's plan to launch approximately 1,600 LEO satellites "technically sound" and comparable to global systems like Starlink.
  • The proposed constellation, orbiting at 650 km altitude, would deliver 4.5–5 Tbps of capacity over India — exceeding Starlink's approved 600 Gbps and Amazon's proposed 3 Tbps.
  • The project carries an estimated price tag of $10–15 billion and could make India only the third country, after the US and China, with a domestically owned LEO broadband platform.
  • IN-SPACe has flagged the proposal's defence value, with discussions underway about hosting military payloads on some satellites.

India's Space Regulator Clears the Path

India's space regulator IN-SPACe has assessed Reliance Jio's plan to build a 1,600-satellite low Earth orbit constellation and found it "technically sound" and comparable to global systems such as SpaceX's Starlink, according to the Economic Times. The evaluation was conducted jointly by IN-SPACe, the Indian Space Research Organisation, and the Wireless Planning and Coordination wing of the Department of Telecommunications.

With this clearance, the government can now extend regulatory backing to Jio at the international level, supporting its filings with the International Telecommunications Union for securing orbital slots and coordinating spectrum rights with other satellite operators. The approval marks a decisive step toward India building its first domestically owned LEO broadband network.

The Scale of Ambition

"Now, we must connect India from the skies."</p> <cite>— Aakash Ambani, Chairman, Reliance Jio</cite> </blockquote> <h2>National Security Underpins the Push</h2> <p>The timing is no coincidence."

The proposed constellation would orbit at approximately 650 kilometres altitude, offering both broadband and direct-to-device connectivity. According to the Outlook Business assessment, Jio's planned capacity of 4.5–5 terabits per second over India would top Starlink's currently approved 600 Gbps and Amazon Kuiper's proposed 3 Tbps, though neither comparison accounts for operational differences in coverage and ground infrastructure.

The project's estimated cost of $10–15 billion (roughly ₹95,000 to ₹1,41,500 crore) makes it one of the largest capital commitments in Indian corporate history. Jio has indicated a two-to-three-year deployment timeline, though analysts at Communications Today have noted that this is "extraordinarily aggressive" by global standards, given that Amazon — with every structural advantage of a $2 trillion company — has deployed only a fraction of its planned Kuiper network in a comparable timeframe.

"Jio connected India on the ground. Now, we must connect India from the skies."

— Aakash Ambani, Chairman, Reliance Jio

The timing is no coincidence. India's Ministry of Home Affairs has been applying heightened scrutiny to foreign satellite operators throughout 2026, raising concerns about signal spillage in border areas and government control over foreign-owned orbital infrastructure during conflict. Starlink's remaining Indian approvals have effectively been frozen by security agencies, despite the company having secured prior clearances from IN-SPACe and the telecom department.

An Indian-owned, Indian-filed constellation sidesteps precisely these concerns. IN-SPACe has separately flagged the defence value of Jio's proposal, with discussions underway about hosting military payloads on some of the satellites — a dual-use model that mirrors approaches taken by SpaceX's Starshield programme.

Competing in a Crowded Orbit

The global LEO satellite race is intensifying. SpaceX operates approximately 9,500–10,000 Starlink satellites, with authorization for up to 12,000 in its first orbital shell. Chinese companies filed for constellations covering more than 200,000 satellites in December 2025 alone. India, by contrast, has had no operational LEO constellation until now.

The satellite unit will be housed under Jio Platforms, alongside the company's other digital assets. The entity has been valued at approximately $148 billion by ICICI Securities, and a planned IPO could create a natural window to raise capital for the constellation's deployment. About 95 percent of Emergent's workforce may be in India, but Jio's satellite constellation would represent an entirely different category of Indian technological ambition — infrastructure that orbits overhead rather than code that runs on screens.

What Remains Uncertain

Critical questions remain. The extent to which Jio will genuinely manufacture satellites domestically versus deploying imported hardware under an Indian filing will determine whether the "self-reliance" framing holds. The company's existing Jio-SES joint venture, which operates in geostationary orbit, adds structural complexity. And at 650 km altitude, Jio's satellites would share orbital shells with Starlink and potentially Kuiper, requiring complex spectrum coordination with established operators. India is a first-time LEO entrant in a neighborhood that already has powerful incumbents.
